GCD and LCM by Plain Factorization

Number TheoryDivisibilityArithmetic
Game: Two numbers are broken into primes, and the biggest number that divides both and the smallest that both divide are read off; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Type two numbers (or products like 12*5*7) and press Compute. Add one factor at a time and guess what changes.
Factorization
Look for the math

Every whole number above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, and that makes the gcd and lcm easy to read off.

Smaller and larger exponents

For every prime, look at its exponent in each number. The gcd takes the smaller exponent and the lcm the larger. The table shows them side by side. The logic test checked this against Euclid’s algorithm for every pair from 1 to 400 and for 20,000 random pairs with a number up to two billion.

gcd × lcm = M × N

For every prime the smaller and the larger of two exponents add up to the same as the exponents themselves: min(a, b) + max(a, b) = a + b. Multiply over all the primes and you get gcd(M, N) · lcm(M, N) = M · N, which is why finding one of them gives the other. The page shows the check under the table.

Building numbers a factor at a time

Adding one factor to a number raises one exponent. If it raises the exponent in the smaller of the two, the gcd grows with it; if it raises the larger, only the lcm grows. Try it: type 360, then 360*7, and watch.

Like the applet, this page reads a text as a whole number or a product of whole numbers joined with *, and writes 0 back for anything else; the page says it handles numbers up to 7,000,000,000, and so does this one.

Try 360 and 84, then add *5 to the second. What happens to the gcd? And to the lcm?
